title: Rebuild a Row From Neighbor Pairs
statement:
Someone had a row of n distinct integers and wrote down every pair of values that stood next to each other: n − 1 pairs in total. Then they lost the row and shuffled the pairs. Inside a pair the two values can be in either order.

Given pairs, rebuild the row and return it. The row read backwards fits the same pairs, so either direction is accepted.

examples.why: 7 and 9 each appear in only one pair, so they are the two ends. From 7 the only way on is 4, then -1, then 9. [9, -1, 4, 7] is accepted too.
Two values, one pair. [2, 5] is also accepted.
The pairs come in any order, so you cannot just chain them as listed: [3, 1] is followed by [1, 2], not by [2, 6].

constraints: All values in the row are distinct, and the pairs come from a real row
hints: Think of each value as a node and each pair as an edge. What shape does that graph have?
It is a simple path. The two ends are the only values that appear in exactly one pair.
Build an adjacency map, start at an end, and keep stepping to the neighbor that is not the value you just came from.

explain.intuition:
Treat values as nodes and pairs as edges. A row is a path: every inner value touches two neighbors, the two ends touch one. So an end is any value whose neighbor list has length 1.

From an end, the walk is forced. Each inner value has two neighbors, and one of them is where you just came from, so the other one is next. A map from value to neighbors makes every step O(1).
steps: Build a map value → list of neighbors from all pairs.
Find a value whose list has exactly one neighbor. It is an end of the row.
Start the row with that end and its only neighbor.
Repeat until the row has n values: look at the neighbors of the last value and append the one that is not the second-to-last value.
pitfalls: Chaining the pairs in the order given. They are shuffled, so a pair is rarely followed by its neighbor.
Using a visited check of neighbor !== previous index instead of comparing values. Compare against the value you came from.
Walking recursively. A row of 100 000 values overflows the call stack; a loop does not.

solutions.title: Scan the pair list at every step
solutions.idea: Find an end by counting appearances, then at each step search all pairs for one that continues from the last value and does not lead back.

solutions.title: Adjacency map and a forced walk
solutions.idea: Map each value to its neighbors. Start from a value with one neighbor and always step to the neighbor you did not come from.

followups: Values may repeat in the row. Is the row still uniquely determined, and what breaks in this approach?
Some pairs are missing, so you get several separate pieces. How would you return every piece?
lcTitle: Restore the Array From Adjacent Pairs
